Les traditions de référence distinguent également les Compétences de Matière Inorganique Elfiques (Elven Inorganic Skills), destinées aux personnages elfes, de leur équivalent employé par les autres peuples. Cette particularité doit être appliquée selon les données effectivement disponibles dans MERP-RMU et les autorisations culturelles retenues.

Orientation des compétences

L'Alchimiste privilégie l'Artisanat, les Connaissances magiques et techniques, les compétences de Perception de la Puissance, de Manipulation de la Puissance et le Développement des Points de Puissance.

Les compétences artisanales doivent correspondre aux objets qu'il souhaite fabriquer. Un enchanteur d'armes possède des besoins différents de ceux d'un préparateur de potions ou d'un spécialiste de l'orfèvrerie. La connaissance des matériaux et des procédés ordinaires demeure importante, même lorsqu'un pouvoir magique intervient pendant la fabrication.

Fabrication et imprégnation

La création d'un objet magique dépend des conditions prévues par les sorts et des règles RMU effectivement appliquées. Le Meneur tient compte du niveau du praticien, des Listes maîtrisées, de la disponibilité des matériaux et des autres exigences mécaniques.

Dans MERP-RMU, l'identité de la profession gagne à être renforcée par la place accordée aux ateliers, à la transmission des savoirs et à la rareté de certaines ressources. Les grandes créations doivent demeurer des entreprises dont la réalisation possède une importance dans la campagne, sans remplacer les mécanismes de fabrication par des limitations arbitraires.

L'imprégnation de sorts relevant d'autres domaines peut justifier la collaboration avec des praticiens de Théurgie ou de Mentalisme, selon les procédés autorisés. La coopération entre plusieurs professions constitue ainsi un élément intéressant de la création magique.

Les objets de pouvoir dans la Terre du Milieu

Une distinction essentielle doit être maintenue entre les objets décrits par Tolkien et les enchantements accessibles aux personnages.

Les Silmarils, les Anneaux de Pouvoir, les grandes œuvres des artisans d'Eregion et certains ouvrages des Nains appartiennent à des traditions dont la portée dépasse souvent celle des capacités ordinaires de l'Alchimiste. Leur puissance, leur origine et leur importance historique ne doivent pas être ramenées automatiquement aux effets des Listes de sorts.

L'Alchimiste de MERP-RMU représente une adaptation ludique des artisans capables de fixer certains pouvoirs dans des objets. Ses créations doivent respecter les limitations mécaniques du système et les traditions culturelles de la campagne.

Alchimiste et Magicien

L'Alchimiste et le Magicien appartiennent tous deux au domaine de l'Essence, avec les mêmes caractéristiques primordiales, mais leurs spécialisations diffèrent profondément.

Le Magicien agit principalement sur les forces élémentaires pour produire des effets directs. L'Alchimiste consacre son savoir à l'étude des matériaux et à la création d'objets capables de conserver des effets magiques.

Cette distinction influe sur leur manière d'aborder les difficultés. Face à une porte ancienne, le Magicien cherchera peut-être à agir sur la matière qui la compose, tandis que l'Alchimiste examinera les mécanismes, les inscriptions et les éventuelles propriétés magiques de l'ouvrage.

Ombre et Corruption

L'Essence n'est pas intrinsèquement corrompue. Toutefois, les objets de pouvoir peuvent devenir des instruments de domination, de violence ou de servitude.

Le Meneur applique les règles de l'Ombre et de la Corruption de MERP-RMU selon les circonstances et les actes accomplis, particulièrement lorsque le personnage cherche à employer des procédés interdits ou à fabriquer des objets destinés à asservir autrui.

La profession prend toute sa dimension lorsque les créations possèdent une histoire, une destination et des conséquences concrètes dans le monde. Les œuvres de l'Alchimiste peuvent servir plusieurs générations ; leur valeur dépend autant de la qualité de l'enchantement que des décisions de ceux qui les fabriquent et les utilisent.

Note au Meneur — Les traditions alchimiques

Les six listes de base proposées à l'Alchimiste dans MERP-UI constituent la configuration de référence de la profession. Elles permettent de jouer immédiatement un Alchimiste selon les règles de Rolemaster Unified, tout en laissant au Meneur la possibilité d'adapter sa formation aux traditions de la Terre du Milieu.

Dans leur adaptation de MERP à Rolemaster Standard System, Whitford Bates et les autres membres du collectif de joueurs envisageaient une approche plus souple : l'Alchimiste pouvait choisir six listes parmi un ensemble plus vaste, certaines traditions dépendant notamment du peuple auquel il appartenait. Les artisans elfes, les forgerons nains et les alchimistes des peuples humains pouvaient ainsi recevoir des formations différentes.

Un artisan elfe pourra privilégier les enchantements délicats, le travail des matériaux organiques et l'incorporation de pouvoirs dans les objets. Un forgeron nain pourra se consacrer aux métaux, aux armes, aux armures et aux propriétés particulières des matériaux. Un alchimiste humain pourra développer davantage la préparation de substances, de potions et d'objets enchantés.

Le collectif distinguait notamment les traditions relatives au travail des matériaux inorganiques et proposait des variantes adaptées aux artisans elfes et aux autres peuples. Ces différences reflétaient des savoir-faire et des héritages culturels que le Meneur peut aujourd'hui intégrer à sa campagne.

Le Meneur peut donc autoriser le remplacement de certaines listes de base proposées par MERP-UI par d'autres listes appropriées à la culture, à l'apprentissage et à l'histoire du personnage. Il détermine ces substitutions avec le joueur lors de la création du personnage, en conservant six listes de base et les règles de développement de RMU.

Les listes officielles disponibles dans RMU Spell Law seront privilégiées lorsqu'elles correspondent à la tradition choisie. Les listes provenant d'autres ouvrages ou adaptations ne seront utilisées que si le Meneur dispose des règles correspondantes et autorise leur emploi.

Cette souplesse permet de représenter la diversité des traditions alchimiques de la Terre du Milieu tout en conservant une base de règles commune.

Alchemist

Matter and Its Enchantments

In a narrow street of Pelargir, a short distance from the warehouses overlooking the quays, a light remains burning long after the shops have closed. Behind an oak door reinforced with iron bands, a man works in a workshop whose windows overlook a small courtyard. Shelves line the walls, laden with crucibles, vials, wooden boxes, and carefully labelled containers. Several precision tools lie upon a long table beside a hearth, where embers glow red beneath the ashes.

Since the middle of the afternoon, the man has been examining a small silver casket brought to him by an officer of Gondor. It was discovered among the ruins of an abandoned house in Ithilien, among the possessions of a family that had left the region several generations earlier. Its lid bears a pattern of interwoven leaves and an inscription whose characters have almost disappeared through wear.

The casket is remarkably well preserved. The silver shows a few traces of tarnish, but its hinges remain intact and the fastening mechanism still works. Inside is a plate of darker metal, secured beneath the lid by four tiny rivets. It is this piece that holds the Alchemist's attention.

After carefully cleaning its surface, he discovers a second inscription, engraved with extraordinary delicacy. Several signs are familiar to him, but their arrangement matches no formula he knows. He consults a manuscript resting upon a lectern, then resumes his examination by lamplight.

His assistant, a young man trained in smithcraft, silently watches him work.

“Is it an enchantment?” he asks at last.

The Alchemist nods. He points out a series of almost invisible lines extending towards the edges of the plate.

“The metal was prepared to receive a magical effect. These lines lead towards the centre of the work, where the power was to be bound. We must discover what spell was placed within it before we attempt to awaken it.”

He asks his assistant to prepare a small quantity of mineral powder and arrange several tools near the hearth. Meanwhile, he studies the marks left by the ancient craftsman. Some correspond to techniques still taught in Gondor; others remind him of works dating from the last centuries of Númenor.

When the preparations are complete, the Alchemist places his hands on either side of the casket. He closes his eyes and directs his attention towards the object's magical properties. The examination is difficult. The power that once inhabited it has weakened with time, and several parts of the inscription have been damaged.

Little by little, however, he begins to discern the structure of an enchantment intended to protect its contents. The magic no longer appears active, but traces of its original pattern can still be perceived.

He straightens and carefully records his observations.

The assistant wishes to know whether they will be able to restore the casket. His master studies the object for some time before replying. The physical damage is relatively slight; painstaking silversmith's work should repair its most fragile parts. Restoring the enchantment will require considerably more research. They will need to identify the materials used, reconstruct the conditions under which it was made, and understand how the ancient craftsman bound the power into the metal.

The officer who entrusted him with the casket had hoped to recover it before the end of the week. The Alchemist will write to him the next day and explain that the examination must continue for several months.

He knows the value of such discoveries. Throughout the lands once governed by the kings of Gondor, ruins still preserve works made by masters whose techniques have sometimes been lost. Each recovered object adds a few more pieces to the understanding of their craft.

As midnight approaches, the man covers the casket with a cloth and closes his workshop ledgers. He instructs his assistant to leave their notes beside the table, then extinguishes the lamps one by one.

Tomorrow they will resume their examination of the inscriptions. The work may demand weeks of comparison, many attempts, and the help of a craftsman able to recognise the alloy employed by the ancient masters. The Alchemist accepts the prospect with the patience of a man who has devoted his life to similar undertakings.

For almost forty years, he has studied the ways in which magic may be joined to materials and preserved within enduring works. His knowledge embraces craftsmanship, the properties of matter, and the disciplines of Essence. He creates certain objects, restores others, and pursues his research into enchantments handed down by earlier generations.

He is an Alchemist, heir to a tradition in which magical power is joined to the skill of the hands and the knowledge of materials.

The Art of Binding Power

In Middle-earth, objects of power occupy a singular place. A sword forged in a vanished kingdom, a jewel preserved since ancient times, or a door whose inscriptions respond to particular conditions may endure for centuries, remaining bound to the events that marked its creation.

The Alchemist devotes his craft to this relationship between matter and magic. Where the Magician chiefly employs Essence to produce an immediate effect, the Alchemist seeks to bind power to a material vessel. His work may produce enchanted weapons, protective equipment, magical preparations, inscriptions, or objects capable of retaining the effects of certain spells.

This vocation demands an exceptionally broad range of knowledge. The success of an enchantment depends upon the powers mastered, but also upon the characteristics of the object that must receive them. Metal, stone, wood, glass, and liquid substances have different properties. Preparing them requires appropriate techniques, sometimes passed down within a craft tradition over many generations.

An Alchemist must therefore be both a practitioner of Essence and a student of matter. He learns to recognise materials, understand methods of manufacture, and establish the conditions needed to associate a magical effect with a work. A poorly fashioned object can ruin weeks of labour, even when its maker possesses sufficient magical knowledge.

Patience is one of the essential qualities of this profession. Some preparations may be completed quickly, but the most demanding enchantments require prolonged investigation, repeated trials, and meticulous execution. A practitioner may have to begin an entire stage again after discovering an imperfection in the vessel or an error in the conditions of the experiment.

This painstaking work gives the finished objects particular value. They embody hours of labour, carefully selected materials, and a body of knowledge whose transmission is sometimes difficult. In regions where practitioners of Essence are rare, a well-made work may become a family heirloom or a treasured possession preserved for generations.

The Alchemist thus develops a deep relationship with his creations. He knows every stage of their making, the difficulties encountered, and the properties he sought to bestow upon them. Some works remain with him for years, while others leave his workshop to serve people whose fate he may never know.

The Great Craftsmen of Ancient Days

The history of Middle-earth preserves the memory of craftsmen whose achievements surpass the abilities of ordinary practitioners. Their works bear witness to traditions in which knowledge of matter, beauty of workmanship, and extraordinary powers were intimately joined.

Among the Valar, Aulë holds a particular place. He knows the substances of which Arda is made and possesses exceptional mastery over the works fashioned by hand. The Dwarves recognise him as their maker and preserve throughout their history a deep devotion to the working of stone and metal.

The Noldor likewise inherited a remarkable tradition of craftsmanship. During their years in Aman, their masters learned to shape metals and gems with extraordinary skill. Fëanor represents the most celebrated expression of that art. His works included achievements of exceptional complexity, but none approached the importance of the three Silmarils, in which he enclosed the light of the Two Trees.

The creation of those jewels remains a unique event in the history of Arda. Their nature and the circumstances of their making lie beyond the powers of an ordinary Alchemist, even one belonging to a people whose magical traditions are exceedingly ancient.

In the Second Age, the craftsmen of Eregion continued certain branches of Noldorin knowledge. Under the leadership of Celebrimbor, the Gwaith-i-Mírdain, the Jewel-smiths, attained remarkable mastery of the crafts. Their relations with the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm encouraged the exchange of techniques and the undertaking of works together.

The Doors of Durin bear witness to this collaboration. Fashioned by the Dwarf Narvi, they bear signs drawn by Celebrimbor in a substance called ithildin, whose inscriptions become visible under particular conditions of light. The precision of the work and the properties of its materials illustrate the joining of two peoples' craftsmanship.

The making of the Rings of Power was an undertaking of a still different nature. The teachings received by the craftsmen of Eregion, Sauron's intervention in the guise of Annatar, and the consequences of these creations hold a central place in the history of the Second Age. The power of these objects and the purposes governing their creation must be distinguished from the enchantments available to an ordinary character.

The Dwarves, for their part, possess traditions closely bound to their Houses and workshops. The weapons, protective equipment, doors, and works of stone made by their masters are enduring witnesses to their knowledge. Their mastery of materials and exacting standards of craftsmanship offer valuable examples to any Alchemist, even when the powers they employ belong to a tradition different from that of Essence.

These inheritances give the profession particular depth. The Alchemist of the Third Age works in a world where many ancient creations survive, although the workshops, masters, and knowledge needed to make them have sometimes vanished long ago.

The Years of Apprenticeship

An Alchemist's training generally begins under a master who possesses both magical knowledge and practical experience of craftsmanship. Some pupils come from families of goldsmiths, smiths, or preparers of substances. Others have received a scholarly education before discovering the possibility of joining the powers of Essence to the materials they study.

The first years are often devoted to the ordinary tasks of the workshop. The apprentice maintains the tools, prepares raw materials, and learns to recognise the characteristics of metals, stones, and other substances used by his master. He discovers methods of measurement, the temperatures required for particular processes, and the precautions essential when working with fragile materials.

Precision soon becomes a habit. A piece intended to receive a mechanism must have exact dimensions; an alloy requires suitable proportions; an inscription must be traced with sufficient regularity to remain legible and satisfy the requirements of the chosen process.

The master also teaches his pupil to identify flaws in a work. An almost invisible crack may compromise the strength of a metal component, while an impurity can alter a material's properties. Experience develops the attention to detail upon which the success of later enchantments will depend.

The study of manuscripts completes this instruction. Alchemical traditions are sometimes preserved in works combining technical observations, descriptions of materials, and magical knowledge. Reading them demands a sound command of languages, numbers, and the methods used to describe manufacturing processes.

The study of Essence is introduced gradually. The pupil begins with disciplines of concentration, perception, and the manipulation of power. The first effects are generally limited, allowing him to understand how magic responds when brought into contact with different vessels.

The difficulty increases when he must maintain an effect during a physical operation. Enchantment sometimes requires the coordination of several movements, exact preparation, and the casting of a spell at the proper moment. The apprentice then discovers that success depends upon the entire process, and that mastery of magic does not excuse careless craftsmanship.

As his knowledge grows, he takes part in the workshop's more complex undertakings. At first, his master entrusts him with preparing the vessels, then with certain stages of the enchantment itself. The first works completed under his own responsibility are often modest objects, but their creation marks an important stage in his training.

Traditions differ in how their most precious teachings are transmitted. Some masters readily share their knowledge with pupils who have demonstrated diligence. Others guard the processes belonging to their family or workshop, requiring many years of service before revealing the details.

These differences profoundly shape the future Alchemist's character. He may become a generous craftsman devoted to passing on knowledge, or an especially reserved practitioner, keenly aware of the value of the secrets entrusted to him.

Matter and the Perfection of Craftsmanship

Choosing materials is one of the Alchemist's first important decisions. An object's properties depend upon its composition, the way it was fashioned, and the treatments to which it has been subjected.

Metals offer particularly rich possibilities. Iron, steel, silver, gold, and the alloys employed by craftsmen possess different qualities. Some are suited to making weapons, others to jewellery or objects whose purpose requires great precision. Metalworking demands careful knowledge of temperatures, impurities, and the processes needed to produce a durable piece.

Stone imposes other requirements. Gems, crystals, and minerals used in precious objects must be examined with care. Their cutting and arrangement may form part of an enchantment process, especially when the object must bear an inscription or retain a particular magical effect.

Organic materials also have an important place. Wood, leather, certain resins, and plant-based preparations can be used to produce objects with properties quite different from those of metal. Their preservation and preparation require knowledge suited to their nature.

The Alchemist learns to understand the relationship between a material and the intended use of the work. Protective equipment meant to be worn for years must withstand movement, moisture, and ordinary wear. A vessel intended to hold a magical preparation must be compatible with the substance it contains. An enchanted weapon must still meet the physical demands of its purpose.

In Middle-earth, certain materials enjoy an extraordinary reputation. Mithril, once mined in Khazad-dûm, is among the most celebrated examples. Its rarity and remarkable properties give it enormous value, particularly after the closing of the ancient mines.

Yet extraordinary materials remain difficult to obtain. An Alchemist must generally work with the resources available in his region, choosing those that meet the requirements of his research. The quality of his art is therefore evident in his ability to make the best use of the substances at hand.

Long years in the workshop develop in some practitioners an almost instinctive appreciation of fine craftsmanship. They recognise the precision of a joint, the balance of a blade, or the delicacy of an engraving before even examining its magical properties.

Such attention lies at the heart of their vocation: enchantment enhances a work whose material quality already possesses value in its own right.

Enchanted Weapons and Protective Equipment

The making of magical weapons and protective equipment is one of the most sought-after branches of alchemy. The kingdoms of Middle-earth have long understood the value of equipment able to withstand the hardships of battle, especially when it is intended to pass from one generation to another.

An Alchemist who chooses this specialisation generally works closely with smiths and armourers. He examines the quality of the materials, the arrangement of the components, and the characteristics of the object before undertaking the magical operations.

Weapon Enchantments allow certain powers to be associated with instruments of war. The available effects depend upon the spells employed and the properties of the work. The practitioner must understand the stresses to which the weapon will be subjected, whether it is a sword worn at the belt, a lance carried by a horseman, or a tool intended to defend a narrow passage.

Armour Enchantments concern protective equipment. Their creation requires particular attention to the strength of the components, how they are assembled, and the way they move with the wearer. Exceptionally wrought armour remains a complex work, its quality depending as much upon the craftsman as upon the power bound to it.

Such objects naturally attract the interest of military leaders, noble families, and renowned warriors. Some wish to protect an heir, while others wish to present a weapon to a companion in recognition of his service. The rewards offered may be considerable, especially when the Alchemist's reputation reaches beyond his own region.

Their creation nevertheless requires time and resources. An enchanted object is not necessarily the product of a single operation; making it may involve several stages, rare materials, and the collaboration of specialised practitioners.

The relationship between the craftsman and the object's future owner is also important. A warlord may seek a weapon whose abilities far exceed the actual needs of his mission, while a traveller may expect magical protection to provide a degree of safety that no equipment can fully guarantee.

The experienced Alchemist learns to discuss such expectations. He recommends suitable materials, explains what the enchantment can accomplish, and reminds his patron of the work's limitations.

A successful creation may remain in the same family for generations. As its origins recede into the past, descendants may forget the details of its making and attribute qualities to it that it never possessed. The Alchemist's work thus becomes part of memory and tradition.

Potions and Preparations

The Alchemist's knowledge also encompasses liquids, gases, and certain prepared substances. This specialisation allows magic to be bound to vessels whose use differs from that of weapons, protective equipment, and solid objects.

The preparation of a potion begins with the selection of its ingredients. The practitioner must know their properties, establish the conditions under which they may be combined, and use suitable containers. Certain preparations require a precise temperature or a sequence of operations whose order is of great importance.

Plants and natural substances offer particularly varied resources. An Alchemist may work with a herbalist or an Animist to identify the required ingredients, while a specialised merchant supplies materials from distant regions.

Magical preparations have many applications. Some are intended for travellers, others for craft operations or for situations in which an effect must be preserved until the moment of its use. Their precise properties remain those of the powers actually employed.

Preservation presents an important difficulty. A substance may lose its qualities if exposed to heat, moisture, or an unsuitable container. Transport also demands precautions, particularly when several different preparations are carried in the same chest.

Working with gases and vapours requires additional care. Certain processes involve heating substances whose fumes may be dangerous. The workshop must therefore have suitable equipment, and the Alchemist ensures that his assistants know the precautions to take.

In Dorwinion, a practitioner may develop remarkable knowledge of oils, plant essences, and preparations made from local crops. In Gondor, some workshops inherit scholarly traditions in which the preparation of substances is joined to medical knowledge and craftsmanship.

This variety makes the Alchemist a particularly valued specialist whenever a magical effect must be preserved in a transportable substance or used on a particular occasion.

Inscriptions and Spell Imbedding

One of the Alchemist's most characteristic disciplines consists of binding a magical effect into an object so that it may be preserved or used at a later time.

This practice demands precise knowledge of the spell concerned, its vessel, and the conditions required for imbedding it. The object must be prepared to receive the power, then subjected to the operations prescribed by the chosen discipline.

Own Realm Imbedding concerns spells belonging to Essence. It allows the practitioner to place certain effects from his own magical tradition into objects, in accordance with the powers he has mastered.

Other Realm Imbedding offers more particular possibilities. It concerns spells belonging to other realms, including Channeling or Mentalism. Their imbedding requires suitable conditions and may call for the participation of another spell user or access to an appropriate magical source.

Such cooperation can lead to complex undertakings. An Alchemist may work alongside a Lay Healer to devise an object intended to aid certain treatments, or seek the assistance of an Animist when an enchantment concerns the forces of nature. The knowledge of both practitioners is then brought together in a single project.

Inscriptions may form part of these processes. An engraving, symbol, or written formula sometimes constitutes an important element in the object's preparation. Knowledge of ancient alphabets and craft traditions consequently becomes valuable.

A distinction must nevertheless be drawn between ordinary writing and inscriptions possessing a genuine magical function. Dwarven runes and the characters employed by Elves are also systems of writing used to convey information and preserve names. Their presence upon an object does not, in itself, give it power.

The Alchemist must therefore understand the relationship between the sign, the material, and the enchantment. An inscription may identify a weapon's owner, recall the name of its maker, or play a part in a particular magical process. Understanding its purpose requires historical knowledge as well as technical expertise.

Objects prepared in this way may take many forms: rings, jewels, staves, wands, weapons, protective equipment, or instruments intended for particular purposes. Their creation reflects the practitioner's traditions, the materials available, and the nature of the desired effect.

The Alchemist's Magical Traditions

The Alchemist's professional teachings are remarkably varied. His training allows him to direct his studies towards several different fields, according to his master's knowledge and the work he intends to undertake.

Some practitioners favour enchantments intended for weapons and protective equipment. Others delve into techniques for working with organic or inorganic materials. Makers of potions devote more time to the study of liquids and gases, while craftsmen specialising in objects of power seek methods for imbedding different spells within them.

Item Analysis holds a particular place among these traditions. It provides the means to understand the magical properties of a work and becomes indispensable when a practitioner seeks to examine an enchantment whose nature is unknown to him.

General Enchantments broaden the scope of creation beyond weapons and armour, allowing objects intended for many different uses to be devised.

The disciplines of Organic Skills and Inorganic Skills deepen the possibilities offered by materials. They concern, respectively, substances whose properties require distinct processes, and their study enriches the knowledge needed to devise magical vessels.

The various forms of Imbedding complete these teachings by allowing certain spells to be placed within objects. They open a field in which the Alchemist's knowledge of Essence must sometimes be joined to that of practitioners belonging to other magical traditions.

This diversity explains why two Alchemists may possess very different abilities despite a common foundation in their training. A workshop master specialising in enchanted weapons will not pursue the same investigations as a maker of potions or a scholar devoted to the analysis of ancient relics.

In certain Elven traditions, the working of inorganic substances is the subject of particular teachings, whose techniques differ from those passed down among other peoples. The opportunities for specialisation must therefore be considered in the light of the character's culture and training.

The Study of Ancient Objects

The search for lost creations is among the most fascinating aspects of the profession. The lands of Eriador, the ancient dwellings of Gondor, and the ruins of the Elven kingdoms still hold objects whose makers vanished centuries ago.

An Alchemist undertaking their study begins by examining their material nature. The composition of a metal, the way a stone was cut, or the marks left by tools may reveal the craft tradition from which an object came. Inscriptions provide further clues, especially when they mention a name, a place, or a purpose.

Magical investigation then complements this examination. Analytical powers may reveal certain properties of an object, the effects it retains, and the conditions under which they may be used. The practitioner also seeks to understand how the enchantment was bound to its vessel.

Such work demands great caution. An ancient object may possess limitations whose meaning has been lost, while a damaged device may respond differently from the way its maker intended. Some works were created to function under particular conditions that no longer exist when they are discovered.

Historical archives consequently become indispensable. A family chronicle, an inventory preserved in a library, or an account of an ancient journey may provide the information needed to identify a work. The Alchemist thus maintains close relations with scholars, archivists, and specialists in ancient languages.

The study of objects of power also confronts him with the decline of knowledge. Understanding how an enchantment works does not necessarily mean possessing the means to reproduce it. Certain materials have disappeared from markets, the workshops that knew how to prepare them have been destroyed, and the masters familiar with the most complex processes died long ago.

This reality gives discoveries particular value. A single technique recovered from a manuscript may permanently enrich a workshop's knowledge. An exceptional object may make it possible to reconstruct part of a lost body of teaching.

For the Alchemist, such investigations often become a vocation in their own right. He gathers the fragments of a scattered inheritance and seeks to preserve what can still be passed down to future generations.

The Workshops of Different Peoples

The practice of alchemy is profoundly influenced by the craft and magical traditions of the cultures of Middle-earth.

Among the Noldor, the profession finds a particularly favourable setting in the legacy of the great Elven craftsmen. A Noldorin Alchemist may have received instruction from masters whose knowledge reaches back to the final centuries of the Second Age, or even earlier times. His work often joins the physical perfection of an object to a deep understanding of the magical properties of its materials.

The Dúnedain of Gondor preserve traditions inherited from Númenor. An Alchemist established in Minas Tirith may devote himself to analysing ancient works, while a practitioner in Pelargir works alongside craftsmen, merchants, and mariners. Objects recovered from the ruins of ancient cities offer abundant opportunities for research.

Among the Dúnedain of the North, the profession remains rare. The scattered communities have preserved some ancient knowledge, but the resources required for the most complex enchantments are difficult to assemble. An Alchemist may devote much of his life to searching for manuscripts and objects originating in the fallen kingdoms of Arnor.

The Dwarves possess extraordinarily rich craft traditions. The working of stone, metals, and gems holds a central place in their culture. Craftsmen capable of joining magical effects to their creations may belong to teachings specific to their people, distinct from the usual training of an Essence Alchemist. Relations between these traditions provide valuable opportunities for exchange and investigation.

In Umbar, certain families descended from the ancient Númenórean settlements preserve techniques and knowledge inherited from earlier centuries. Alchemists serving the great houses may work upon objects intended for navigation, protection, or war. Their research is sometimes subject to the political interests of their patrons.

In Dorwinion, natural resources and trade encourage practices involving liquids, oils, and particular preparations. An Alchemist from this region may have close ties with producers, herbalists, and merchants who travel the roads of Rhovanion.

In the eastern and southern regions, other traditions of making may have been passed down independently of the great teachings of the West. Their techniques, materials, and relationship with objects of power reflect the history of the peoples who developed them.

The character's cultural origins thus profoundly influence the nature of his workshop, the knowledge available to him, and the way he regards the works he creates.

The Master and His Workshop Companions

An Alchemist's work often takes place in a setting where several people possess complementary skills. A master craftsman directs the operations, apprentices prepare materials, and more experienced journeymen carry out the stages requiring particular skill.

The division of responsibilities varies between workshops. Some practitioners personally perform every stage of a work, from preparing its vessel to completing the enchantment. Others work with smiths, goldsmiths, or specialised preparers, entrusting them with certain material operations.

This collaboration demands considerable trust. A mistake made during the first stages may ruin an enchantment begun several weeks later. The master must therefore know his assistants' abilities and provide the instructions needed to carry out the work properly.

Personal relationships play an important part in workshop life. Apprentices sometimes spend many years beside the same master, sharing his successes, his difficulties, and the long periods during which research seems to yield nothing. Some become his successors; others leave to establish workshops of their own.

The question of trade secrets may lead to tension. A process handed down within a family sometimes represents the outcome of several generations of research. Its owner is reluctant to reveal it, especially when it might be used by competitors or people whose intentions he distrusts.

The Alchemist may also work with spell users of other professions. Imbedding a particular power sometimes requires the participation of a practitioner whose knowledge complements his own. Such undertakings can lead to lasting collaborations founded upon trust and mutual recognition of each other's skills.

Over the years, the workshop thus becomes a place of transmission. Its tools, records, and unfinished works preserve the memory of successive undertakings. The departure of a master or the loss of an apprentice often means far more than the loss of a pair of working hands.

Power, Possession, and the Shadow

Objects of power occupy a particular place in the history of peoples, for their power may survive their makers by centuries. Such endurance gives them considerable value, but may also awaken the covetousness of those who wish to possess them.

The history of the Silmarils recalls how an exceptional creation may become the object of destructive attachment. Their making bears witness to Fëanor's genius, but the oath sworn by him and his sons after their theft contributes to many tragedies. The desire to recover or retain the jewels ultimately becomes entangled with the fate of several peoples.

The Rings of Power provide an even more direct example of the dangers of enchantment. Sauron seeks to use the knowledge of the craftsmen of Eregion to establish his dominion. The power bestowed upon certain objects thus becomes the instrument of a design whose consequences mark the entire history of the Second and Third Ages.

For the Alchemist, these accounts carry profound meaning. The quality of a work and the extent of its power do not, by themselves, determine the worth of the undertaking that brought it into being. The maker's intentions, the object's intended use, and the means employed to create it deserve equally careful consideration.

This responsibility is also evident in ordinary commissions. A lord wishes to acquire a weapon that will give him a decisive advantage over his enemies; a merchant requests an object intended to conceal particular activities; a patron demands an enchantment whose consequences might threaten innocent people.

The Alchemist must then decide whether to place his knowledge at the service of such undertakings. The rarity of his skills sometimes gives him the means to refuse, yet some masters remain dependent on the families or authorities that support their workshops.

The search for lost knowledge presents another temptation. An ancient work may promise to teach processes of remarkable power, though its origins remain obscure. An ambitious practitioner may be tempted to continue his experiments despite his masters' warnings, convinced that his knowledge will allow him to control the consequences.

The magic of Essence belongs to a discipline of knowledge and craftsmanship. Employing it for domination or corrupt practices nevertheless makes the practitioner responsible for his actions.

The Alchemist must therefore learn to distinguish the work he wishes to accomplish from the power he desires to possess. The objects he creates may outlive him by many years, and the consequences of their use may reach far beyond the intentions that governed their making.

The Alchemist Through the Ages

The Alchemist's place in Middle-earth depends greatly upon the Age chosen for the campaign.

In the First Age, the traditions of the Noldor provide a particularly rich setting for craftsmen capable of joining their knowledge of matter to extraordinary powers. An Elven Alchemist may have learned his art from masters whose techniques date back to their years in Aman. The kingdoms of Beleriand contain workshops where weapons, gems, and precious objects are fashioned with remarkable care. Yet the wars against Morgoth bring about the destruction of many dwellings and the loss of knowledge that will never be fully recovered.

In the Second Age, Eregion is one of the great centres of creation. Relations between Noldorin craftsmen and the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm encourage the exchange of knowledge and the undertaking of works together. The teachings of Celebrimbor and the Gwaith-i-Mírdain attain extraordinary depth, but Sauron's intervention leads to events whose consequences transform Middle-earth for ages to come. In Númenor, the craft and scholarly traditions also undergo considerable growth before the Downfall destroys much of that inheritance.

In the Third Age, the profession assumes a different character. The works of ancient times survive, while masters capable of understanding or reproducing them have become rare. In Gondor, certain practitioners study objects handed down from Númenor or recovered from the ruins of ancient cities. Among the Elves, older traditions continue to be preserved. Human Alchemists sometimes devote most of their lives to recovering techniques of which they possess only a few fragments. The advancing Shadow also demands great caution in the use and transmission of magical knowledge.

In the Fourth Age, the restoration of the Reunited Kingdom opens new possibilities. Roads become safer, exchanges between communities develop, and workshops can resume work interrupted by the wars. An Alchemist may help preserve ancient creations, train new pupils, or seek techniques useful in rebuilding. The gradual departure of the Elves lends particular importance to the knowledge that can still be passed on to the peoples remaining in Middle-earth.

Each Age thus offers a different way to portray the profession. The Alchemist of the First Age inhabits a world where the great arts of the Eldar remain alive; one of the Second Age may take part in the flourishing workshops of Eregion and their exchanges with Númenor. In the Third Age, he often works among the remnants of vanished traditions, while his successor in the Fourth contributes to preserving and renewing the knowledge needed by generations yet to come.

Leaving the Workshop

The Alchemist's calling seems naturally bound to a settled workplace, where tools, materials, and manuscripts remain close at hand. Yet his investigations frequently lead him beyond the dwellings in which he was trained.

A master may ask him to seek a rare substance, meet a craftsman whose techniques differ from his own, or examine an object discovered in a distant region. An ancient chronicle mentions a lost workshop, while a weapon found among the ruins of a fortress displays properties he wishes to understand.

Some journeys arise from personal necessity. An important undertaking has failed and the character seeks to discover why. His master has disappeared after embarking on a dangerous expedition, or an object made in his workshop has been stolen. An Alchemist may also leave home after refusing to continue research on behalf of a patron whose intentions trouble him.

Life upon the roads demands considerable adaptation. The character must learn to select indispensable tools, protect fragile substances, and temporarily set aside work requiring a fully equipped workshop. Certain operations become impossible while travelling, while others can be performed with a reduced assortment of equipment.

Encounters with craftsmen from different regions gradually enrich his knowledge. A Dwarven smith shows him an unfamiliar metalworking technique; a goldsmith of Gondor helps him recognise an ancient design; a herbalist from Dorwinion reveals the properties of a substance used in a particular preparation.

Within a company of adventurers, the Alchemist brings valuable knowledge of objects, materials, and magical phenomena. He helps examine weapons and protective equipment they recover, investigates the properties of ancient relics, and assists his companions in understanding the dangers associated with certain enchantments.

His ability to create, however, depends upon the conditions available to him. Journeys do not always provide the time, materials, or facilities required for the most demanding undertakings. This constraint gives particular importance to periods of rest, when the character can return to a workshop or prepare materials for future expeditions.

The experience of adventure also transforms his relationship with objects. A weapon he once regarded chiefly as a technical achievement becomes a memorial to a companion fallen in battle. A jewel passed from generation to generation acquires a personal value that no magical analysis could measure.

The character thus discovers that his creations have a place in the lives of those who use them. Their importance depends as much upon the events in which they play a part as upon the enchantments they contain.

Playing an Alchemist

The Alchemist offers the opportunity to portray a character whose knowledge unites craftsmanship, the sciences, and mastery of Essence. His cultural background, training, and the circumstances in which he discovered his art nevertheless determine the manner in which he pursues that vocation.

A young scholar of Gondor may have grown up in a family of goldsmiths before receiving instruction from a master specialising in objects of power. A Noldorin Alchemist may be continuing research begun several centuries earlier, while a practitioner from Umbar works in a workshop maintained by an influential house. A craftsman from Dorwinion may devote his studies to substances and preparations whose ingredients come from his country's trade routes.

The character's relationship with his master is an important part of his history. Was he taught generously, or did he spend many years earning access to the most precious knowledge? Is there an unfinished work he has sought to complete since his mentor's death? Did an earlier creation cause an accident whose memory still remains with him?

His character will depend greatly upon the experience gained during his training. Some Alchemists develop great patience, accustomed to devoting weeks to painstaking work. Others become especially demanding towards the craftsmen who assist them, convinced that the slightest negligence can compromise an entire undertaking.

The success of their creations may also foster considerable pride. A practitioner whose works have become widely renowned may come to regard his own methods as the only ones worth following. Conversely, an Alchemist who has suffered several serious failures may hesitate to undertake new research, despite the breadth of his knowledge.

His relationship with his creations deserves particular attention. Some regard each object as a personal work to which they remain attached even after giving it to its owner. Others seek technical perfection above all and readily pass their creations to those who will know how to use them.

The profession is particularly well suited to campaigns involving ancient investigations, ruins, objects of power, and lost craft traditions. It also offers many possibilities when characters must prepare an expedition, identify an enchantment, or find the means of making an object essential to their undertaking.

Over the course of his life, the Alchemist will discover that the endurance of a work does not guarantee the survival of its maker's memory. Some objects outlast the centuries while the names of those who fashioned them have long been forgotten. The knowledge he passes on, the pupils he trains, and the decisions he makes will give his legacy a meaning that reaches beyond the power of the enchantments he creates.

Gamemaster's Notes — The Alchemist in MERP-RMU

The Alchemist is a pure Essence spell user specialising in the creation, analysis, and enchantment of objects.

His prime stats are Empathy (Em) and Reasoning (Re). Empathy is the realm stat for Essence, while Reasoning represents the abilities needed to design objects, analyse materials, and carry out complex magical processes.

Spell Lists

The Alchemist possesses an important distinguishing feature: he selects six Base Spell Lists from nine professional traditions. His opportunities for specialisation are therefore broader than those of professions with six fixed Base Lists.

The six selected Lists become the profession's Base Lists. The others retain the development conditions established by the rules; they do not automatically become additional Base Lists.

The reference traditions also distinguish Elven Inorganic Skills, intended for Elven characters, from their equivalent used by other peoples. This particular feature must be applied in accordance with the data actually available in MERP-RMU and the cultural permissions adopted for the campaign.

Skill Development Priorities

The Alchemist favours Crafting, Magical and Technical Lore, Power Perception, Power Manipulation, and Power Point Development skills.

Craft skills should correspond to the objects he intends to make. An enchanter of weapons has different needs from a potion maker or a specialist in goldsmithing. Knowledge of materials and ordinary manufacturing processes remains important even when magical power is employed during the creation process.

Creation and Imbedding

The creation of a magical object depends upon the conditions laid down by the spells and the RMU rules actually in use. The Gamemaster takes account of the practitioner's level, the Lists he has mastered, the availability of materials, and any other mechanical requirements.

In MERP-RMU, the profession's identity benefits from the importance given to workshops, the transmission of knowledge, and the rarity of certain resources. Great creations should remain undertakings whose completion matters within the campaign, without replacing the crafting mechanics with arbitrary restrictions.

Imbedding spells from other realms may justify collaboration with practitioners of Channeling or Mentalism, according to the permitted processes. Cooperation between several professions can thus become an interesting part of magical creation.

Objects of Power in Middle-earth

An essential distinction must be maintained between the objects described by Tolkien and the enchantments available to player characters.

The Silmarils, the Rings of Power, the great works of the craftsmen of Eregion, and certain creations of the Dwarves belong to traditions whose scope often exceeds the ordinary abilities of an Alchemist. Their power, origin, and historical importance should not automatically be reduced to the effects of Spell Lists.

The MERP-RMU Alchemist represents a game adaptation of craftsmen capable of binding certain powers into objects. His creations must respect the system's mechanical limitations and the cultural traditions of the campaign.

Alchemist and Magician

The Alchemist and the Magician both belong to the realm of Essence and share the same prime stats, but their specialisations differ profoundly.

The Magician primarily acts upon elemental forces to produce direct effects. The Alchemist devotes his knowledge to the study of materials and the creation of objects capable of retaining magical effects.

This distinction shapes the way they approach difficulties. Faced with an ancient door, the Magician might seek to act upon the material of which it is made, while the Alchemist examines its mechanisms, inscriptions, and any magical properties it may possess.

Shadow and Corruption

Essence is not inherently corrupt. Nevertheless, objects of power may become instruments of domination, violence, or servitude.

The Gamemaster applies MERP-RMU's Shadow and Corruption rules according to the circumstances and the actions undertaken, especially when a character seeks to employ forbidden processes or create objects intended to enslave others.

The profession comes fully into its own when creations have a history, a purpose, and tangible consequences in the world. The Alchemist's works may serve several generations; their worth depends as much upon the quality of their enchantments as upon the decisions of those who make and use them.

Gamemaster's Note — Alchemical Traditions

The six Base Spell Lists offered to the Alchemist in MERP-UI constitute the profession's default configuration. They allow an Alchemist to be played immediately using Rolemaster Unified rules, while leaving the Gamemaster free to adapt the character's training to the traditions of Middle-earth.

In their adaptation of MERP to Rolemaster Standard System, Whitford Bates and the other members of the players' collective envisaged a more flexible approach: an Alchemist could choose six lists from a wider selection, with some traditions depending in particular on the people to which the character belonged. Elven artisans, Dwarven smiths, and alchemists of the Mannish peoples could thus receive different training.

An Elven artisan might favour delicate enchantments, the working of organic materials, and the embedding of powers in objects. A Dwarven smith might devote their craft to metals, weapons, armour, and the particular properties of materials. A human alchemist might focus more on preparing substances, potions, and enchanted objects.

The collective distinguished, in particular, traditions concerned with working inorganic materials and proposed variants suited to Elven artisans and other peoples. These differences reflected crafts and cultural inheritances that the Gamemaster may incorporate into a campaign today.

The Gamemaster may therefore permit some of the Base Spell Lists offered by MERP-UI to be replaced with others appropriate to the character's culture, apprenticeship, and history. Such substitutions are agreed with the player during character creation, while retaining six Base Spell Lists and RMU's skill development rules.

Official lists available in RMU Spell Law should be preferred wherever they suit the chosen tradition. Lists from other books or adaptations should be used only if the Gamemaster has access to the relevant rules and permits their use.

This flexibility makes it possible to represent the diversity of alchemical traditions in Middle-earth while retaining a common rules framework.
